en: Child, tell me simply
whom your heart desires.
Choose a bridegroom to your heart's liking—
there are so many of your own people.
Toward the moon in the sky
do not stretch your hand.
I want him
who gave me the honor of a servant,
the storm-fallen datura flower
that he lifted from the dust with his right hand.
O Lord, O Lord,
weave a garland of that flower,
wear it, wear it around your own neck,
do not, do not let it go in vain.
Searching, searching through seven lands,
at last in this place
by fortune I found you—so I am saved.
O Mother, those words indeed are good.
You know the spell,
chant the spell
and bring him to me.
No, nothing will remain, nothing will remain,
nothing at all, nothing at all.
If all of mine is spent,
all is spent,
only then shall I truly live
for all time,
when nothing will remain.
That I have something to give—
it was this one truth
they all together made me forget—
today I know I am no luckless woman;
I will give, I will give, I will give,
I will give myself away utterly.
I have no fear anymore.
Chant your spell, chant your spell,
bring the monk to this unhonored woman's side;
she alone will give him honor—
can anyone else give such honor?
Child, you are the treasure torn from my breast.
At your word I have set out
on the path of sin, a sinful woman.
O holy great soul,
however great the power of my offense,
the power of your forgiveness
is greater many times over.
I shall do you dishonor—
yet I bow, yet I bow, yet I bow.
Hold me guilty.
The pale blossom fallen in the dust—
hold it beneath your feet.
This basket brimming with offenses—
empty it with your own hand,
and then into that empty basket
pour your mercy—
hold me guilty.
You are high, I am small;
I will catch you in a snare—
in my offense.
My fault—your virtue
will make it free of stain—
stringing all my flaws on forgiveness,
wear them around your neck.
What boundless courage you have, girl.
My courage!
His courage has no equal.
The words no one could say,
he spoke them, how simply—
Give me water.
That little utterance—
how great its radiance;
it lit up my whole life.
A black stone lay pressed upon my breast;
he pushed it away—
and a stream of nectar welled up.
Who are they passing by—
monks robed in yellow?
Mother, there he goes,
ahead of them all!
He did not look back, he did not look back—
this new creation of his own hands
he did not turn to see again!
This dust, this dust, this dust alone is your
own!
Luckless woman, who brought you into the light
for only a single instant!
You must remain in the dust,
beneath everyone's feet.
O child, I cannot bear to see your sorrow—
I will bring him, I will bring him, I will bring him
by chanting the spell.
Chant the cruelest spell of all,
coil upon coil, leaving its mark,
let it wind itself around his mind.
Wherever he goes,
never will he escape me—
he cannot, he cannot.
If he goes to the ocean shore, let him go—
let him come again, let him come back.
I will keep a seat spread
in my heart.
I will wet the dust of his path
with the water of my tears.
If he goes to the mountain peak, let him go—
let him come back, let him come back.
I will stay hidden in the mountain cave,
I will call to him—
my dream around his waking
will remain, encircling.
Do not worry—
here, look at my magic mirror;
when you dance with it in your hand
you will see what state has befallen him.
Now come, come, child of Rudra Bhairava,
awaken the tandava dance.
Look there—clouds have massed in the west;
The spell will work, Mother, it will work—
the monk's dry austerities will blow away
like withered leaves.
The lamp will go out, the road will turn dark;
a bird whose nest the storm has broken
will circle and circle and fall at my door.
My breast trembles and trembles;
lightning flickers within my mind.
Far off the sea seems to have surged up foaming—
it has no bottom, no shore.
The spell will work, Mother, it will work.
Shame! Fie, fie—shame!
Raising both arms to the sky,
whom is he cursing?
He lashes himself with a whip of fire,
as if driving a spear into his own heart.
O child, if you grow desperate already,
what will your state be in the end?
I will not look, I will not look,
I will not look at your mirror.
My heart bursts, it bursts, oh,
my heart bursts.
What a terrible whirlwind of sorrow—
will the great forest tree be flung to the dust,
will its sky-piercing glory be broken?
I will not look, I will not look at your mirror.
No, no, no.
That is best, Mother, that is best.
Let your spell be, let your—
no more need, no need, no need.
No, no, no—chant the spell, chant your spell—
there is no path left anymore!
He will come, he will come, he will come,
he will come to the border of my life and death.
In the deep of night the wayfarer will arrive;
with the burning of my breast I
will light the little lamp—
he will come.
With sorrow I will quench your sorrow.
I will bathe you in the fathomless waters
of immense pain.
I will set my world aflame;
the soot of this delusion will be purged—
the pang of death I will lay at your
feet as an offering.
O Mother, at last it seems
his seat has been shaken.
There—he is coming, coming, coming.
What was far away, a hundred thousand leagues away,
what lay beyond the moon and sun—
there—he is coming, coming, coming—
my breast quakes as in an earthquake.
Dense black clouds behind him,
lightning flashing on every side.
Wrapped around and around his body,
a girdle of fire,
like the blaze of Shiva's fire of wrath.
Your spell-words, taking the shape of a black she-serpent,
roar with venomous breath,
defiling his holy flame.
Hungry love has no mercy,
it has no fear, no shame.
Cruel is my vow;
I will not accept defeat, will not accept defeat—
I will bind him in bonds of enchantment,
wrap him in my own laughter and weeping.
Look there—he has crossed the river—
he walks alone on the path through the dense forest,
as if nothing lies before his eyes—
no truth, no falsehood;
no good, no evil.
She has not woken yet, not woken—
the she-serpent who dwells in the nether deep.
Sound, sound, sound, flute—sound
the vast dread melody of the underworld;
wake and rise, black she-serpent of enchantment—
O give ear to my spell—
pull, pull, pull, pull.
Call him with your venomous roar—
coil, coil, coil, coil.
Come out of your cavern,
cross the seven seas.
Bind him and bring him—
pull, pull, pull, pull.
The she-serpent has woken, woken, woken—
there she has begun to coil, begun, begun—
the pull of enchantment has pulled, pulled, pulled—
bound and brought him, bound and brought him, bound and brought him.
Now summon him with the dance—
take up the song, all of you.
Come, all of you, come and join,
band of yoginis.
come, all of you, come,
come, all of you, come,
come, all of you, come.
As a dream comes from the dense depths of sleep,
so rise and come, come.
As fire blazes from the breast of the shami branch,
so you—come, come.
Tearing the black cloud's ban in the northeast sky,
as lightning comes all at once,
so come striking a flash into the depths of my heart—
come, you; come, you; come, come.
When the dark sends its call in silent signs,
as Orion comes into the evening sky,
so you come, you come, come.
On the far peak of the snow mountain,
when the ascetic Baishakh sends forth his spell,
melting the hard dense snow in fierce heat,
as the flood-stream comes down—
so you come, you come, come.
